item.title: Metrwnos Chatbot
item.description:
The problem

Most people who contact a law firm are not ready to hire a lawyer yet. They have a question: about a contract, a dispute, an inheritance, and they want a quick, understandable answer before committing to a paid consultation. For a small firm like Meter we Nos, answering those questions manually eats into billable time, and ignoring them loses potential clients.

Why a chatbot, and why now (Nov 2024)

A year ago this would have been a hard sell. Generic chatbots gave generic answers, and no law firm can afford a bot that improvises legal advice. What changed in 2024 is that retrieval-augmented generation became practical and cheap: the model answers from the firm’s own indexed legal documents instead of its imagination, and fast, low-cost models like Gemini Flash make per-query costs negligible.

The business case is simple:

  • First contact runs 24/7. Prospective clients get an immediate answer in Egyptian Arabic instead of waiting for office hours.
  • Lawyers stop repeating themselves. The most common questions get consistent answers drawn from the firm’s own material, freeing lawyer time for cases that actually need a lawyer.
  • Better-qualified consultations. By the time someone books a session, the basics are already covered, so the intake queue fills with real cases rather than FAQ traffic.

System & Architecture

Built as an AI engineering project around a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline:

  • LLM & Embeddings: Google Gemini (gemini-1.5-flash) through LangChain’s RetrievalQA.
  • Vector Retrieval: FAISS index over a corpus of Egyptian legal documents.

What I did

  • Designed and implemented the RAG pipeline end to end: document indexing, vector retrieval, and answer generation.
  • Wrote the system prompt so responses come back as clear Egyptian Arabic legal explanations, suitable for talking to clients rather than lawyers.
  • Built the Streamlit prototype and the client intake flow around it.

Demo Walkthrough

The demo below (v0.3) shows the chatbot answering Egyptian legal questions and walking through the intake flow:

Outcome

Delivered a working prototype through three demo iterations (v0.1 to v0.3), enough to show the firm that document-grounded LLMs can realistically handle legal intake for a boutique practice.

item.title: EVNTO
item.description:
The problem

At Mansoura University, activities run by different volunteer teams and IEEE societies had no shared home — students had to track each team’s own channel to find and book anything, with no single place to see what was happening across campus. EVNTO, built with the IEEE Vectories team, was our attempt at that missing centralized layer.

Constraints

This was a student-team concept project rather than a funded product build: our evidence base was a competitive review of similar booking/event apps plus a survey we ran among students, not a live pilot with real bookings. The resulting report was meant to justify and steer a build, not to report on one that had already shipped.

What I did

I worked on the research that shaped the product decisions: reviewing how comparable activity/event platforms handled discovery and booking, then running and analysing a student survey to check which of those patterns actually mattered to our own campus audience versus which were just assumptions. Those findings fed directly into the recommendations for how EVNTO’s booking flow and information architecture should work.

What I’d credit

The concrete output was the research report and its recommendations, which the team then used as the basis for prototyping — I don’t have adoption or usage numbers to point to, since it stayed at the concept and prototype stage. What stuck with me was how much a “just build it” instinct benefits from being slowed down by even a small, deliberately-designed survey first.

Team repo on GitHub.

item.title: AQSA
item.description:
The problem

Early-stage founders rarely have a research budget, a forecasting tool, or a team that can build a chatbot on day one — yet they need the same category of decision support that funded startups take for granted. AQSA (“AI for Startups”) was our research project’s answer to that gap: a single concept bundling three things a startup might otherwise assemble piecemeal — a generative chatbot for founder-facing Q&A, an automated data analyser, and a forecasting module.

Constraints

This was a research project, not a funded engineering effort: one semester, a small team, no production users, and no access to real startup data at scale. That shaped the project from the start — the deliverable was a coherent system design and a working proof-of-concept, not a hardened product with measured business outcomes. Being precise about that distinction matters more to me now than it did at the time.

What I did

My focus was the product and system framing: defining what each of the three modules needed to do for a founder, how they’d hand information to one another (chat → analysis → forecast, and back), and where the practical limits of a semester project sat. I worked through the startup workflows the tool was meant to support, and helped shape the analyser and forecasting pieces into something concrete enough for the team to prototype against, alongside the generative chatbot component.

What I’d credit

The project’s real output was the concept and prototype, not a validated product — it’s an archived research effort, and I don’t have production metrics to point to. What it did give me was an early, hands-on look at how the three pillars I still care about — conversational AI, forecasting, and data-driven decision support — fit together as a single system, which is a good part of why I frame my current work the way I do now.

Documented in more depth in the published research report.

item.title: Grow Registration Form
item.description:
The problem

Long registration forms get blamed for drop-off, and the usual fix is “reduce the number of steps.” Grow’s registration form was the case study I used to test whether that assumption actually holds — or whether something else was really driving the effort users felt.

Constraints

This was purely a UX research exercise — no access to Grow’s real signup funnel data, so the work was grounded in usability heuristics and existing research on form design rather than live conversion numbers.

What I did

I went through the existing registration flow step by step and evaluated what each step actually asked of the user — not just how many steps there were, but the type of effort involved (recalling information, making a decision, verifying something) at each one. That reframing became the core of the recommendations: step count is a weak proxy for effort, and it’s what happens within a step, more than how many steps exist, that predicts where users get stuck.

What I’d credit

The output was a set of concrete recommendations for restructuring the form’s steps by the kind of effort they demand, not a measured before-and-after. It left me with a rule of thumb I still use when a form, or an onboarding flow, feels “too long”: count the decisions, not the steps.

Full write-up on Behance.

item.title: Ecommerce Checkout Process
item.description:
The problem

A complicated multi-step checkout is one of the most common reasons ecommerce carts get abandoned right at the point a store has already done the hard work of getting someone to want to buy. This project — a case study for an ecommerce client — set out to make that last step less costly.

Constraints

This was a UX research and design engagement, not an engineering one — the deliverable was a redesigned flow and the reasoning behind it, not a shipped storefront. I didn’t have access to the store’s actual abandonment analytics, so the work leaned on established checkout-UX research and heuristic evaluation rather than a live before/after test.

What I did

I mapped the existing checkout step by step, looking for where it asked users for more than the current step needed, where it introduced friction (forced account creation, unclear progress, redundant fields), and where trust signals were missing. From there I redesigned the flow to be simpler and more seamless, with the explicit goal of getting a customer from cart to confirmed order with as little resistance as possible — and getting them back again next time.

What I’d credit

The deliverable was a full simplified checkout flow, not a production A/B test, so I can’t claim a measured lift in conversions. What it sharpened for me was a habit I still apply to any interface, ML-powered or not: friction shows up step by step, and removing it is a design problem before it’s ever a technical one.

Full case study on Behance.

item.title: Inspiring Art App
item.description:
The problem

Discovering art in a given city — nearby exhibitions, an artist’s back-catalogue, a bit of context on a piece — is scattered across gallery websites, listings pages, and word of mouth. Inspiring Art was a mobile app concept aimed at putting that discovery experience in one place.

Constraints

This was a UX design concept, not a built and shipped app — the deliverable was the interaction design and screens for how someone would browse exhibitions, masterpieces, and artist bios, not a functioning product with real content behind it.

What I did

I designed the core flows for finding a nearby exhibition, browsing notable works, and reading artist bios, aiming for something closer to browsing a well-curated feed than filling out a gallery’s search form. The emphasis throughout was low-friction discovery — the app should surface something interesting before the user has to know what they’re looking for.

What I’d credit

The deliverable was the app concept and its screens, not a live product with usage data, so this stays a design exercise in my history rather than a build claim. It’s one of the earlier projects where I noticed how much “discovery” interfaces — recommend something before being asked — recur across very different products, art included. That’s a thread that’s stayed relevant to how I think about recommendation systems today.

Full concept on Behance.

item.title: TStore Product Details
item.description:
The problem

TStore’s product details page — the page a shopper lands on right before deciding to buy — was the focus of this project: does it give someone enough information to decide quickly, and does it make them want to come back.

Constraints

This was UX research and redesign work on an existing page, not a rebuilt storefront — the deliverable was a reworked product details page and the reasoning behind it, evaluated against usability principles rather than live sales data.

What I did

I reviewed the existing page against what actually drives a purchase decision at that stage — clear product information, trust signals, and an easy path to checkout — and reworked the layout and content around those priorities rather than around what was easiest to build. Loyalty was treated as part of the same problem: a page that’s clear and trustworthy the first time is also the one a customer is willing to come back to.

What I’d credit

The output was a redesigned product details page, not a measured lift in sales or repeat purchases — I don’t have TStore’s data to point to. It’s a small, early example of a pattern I keep coming back to: good UX and good business outcomes are usually the same design problem, described from two different angles.
